title: Broker vs. Direct Lender: Pros and Cons
seo_title: Broker vs. Direct Lender: Pros and Cons | Fidelity Funding
meta_description: Broker vs direct lender for small business funding: speed, choice, cost, control and when each route makes sense, with an honest look at the trade-offs.
keywords: business loan broker pros and cons
dek: Neither path is always better. The right one depends on how well you fit a single lender's box and how much shopping you want to do yourself.
intro: You need funding, and you can get it two ways: apply directly to a lender, or go through a broker who submits you to several. Marketing from both sides makes it sound obvious. Direct lenders say they cut out the middleman; brokers say they shop the market for you.

In reality, both have clear strengths and real drawbacks. This guide compares them across the things that matter most, including cost, choice, speed and control, and ends with a few situations where each one tends to be the smarter move.

paragraphs: A direct lender is the company that underwrites and funds the money. You apply to them, they make a decision, and you deal with them for the life of the agreement. Banks, credit unions and online lenders all fall into this group.

A broker is an intermediary. It takes your application, decides which funding partners may fit, submits your file and helps you compare what comes back. The contract is still signed with the funding partner, not with the broker. Fidelity Funding is in this second group, connecting businesses with its network of funding partners.

Online direct lenders sit somewhere in between. They are lenders, so there is no broker involved, but they often move faster than banks and focus on cash-flow data. Treat them as one more option to compare, not as a separate category with its own rules.

sections.h2: Where direct lenders have the edge
paragraphs: Going direct can mean fewer hands on your file and, in some cases, lower cost, since there is no broker commission layered into the deal. If you already bank with an institution that knows your business, they may offer good terms and a simple process, especially for a straightforward term loan or line of credit.
You also have one point of contact for servicing. Questions about payments, payoffs or renewals go to the same company that made the decision.
bullets: No intermediary commission in the price
Existing banking relationships can help with approval and terms
Single relationship for servicing and renewals
Best fit when your profile matches the lender's standard box

paragraphs: The main advantage is reach. One application can be reviewed by multiple funding partners with different appetites: some focus on strong revenue, others on thin credit, others on a specific industry or product. A direct application to a single lender is a single yes or no.

Brokers also save time for owners who would rather run the business than compare fifteen websites. A funding specialist can explain offers side by side, point out differences in total payback and fees, and handle the document back and forth.
bullets: Access to many funding partners from one application
Matching for unusual or imperfect profiles
Help comparing offers in plain language
Often a faster path to a first answer

sections.h2: The honest downsides on each side
paragraphs: Brokers are typically compensated through commissions or fees, which can raise the total cost versus a direct deal and can create a pull toward the higher-paying product. That is why disclosure matters. Some brokers are also vague about who funds the deal until late in the process.

Direct lenders have their own limits. Each one has fixed credit and revenue requirements, and a decline means starting over elsewhere. Applying to many lenders yourself can mean several hard inquiries, a lot of duplicate paperwork and wasted weeks, especially if timing is tight.

Another cost to weigh is your own time. Filling out multiple applications, uploading the same documents repeatedly and following up with each underwriter can add up to many hours. If you value your time at what your business earns an hour, a broker's convenience may be worth more than it seems, or it may not, depending on the offers.

Say you run a restaurant with solid deposits but a personal credit score that took a hit during a slow year. A bank might decline you on credit alone, and applying to five online lenders costs you a week and several inquiries. A broker could send the same file to partners that weigh revenue more heavily, and you may end up with two or three options to compare.

Flip it: you own a profitable accounting firm with strong credit and a ten-year relationship with a local bank. A direct term loan or line of credit may be cheaper and simple. Going through a broker adds little. These are illustrations; real results vary by funding partner and underwriting.

sections.h2: How to decide, and what to insist on either way
paragraphs: Start by asking whether your profile matches a conventional lender. If so, try your own bank first. If you are not sure, if you need speed, or if you have been declined, a broker conversation is a low-cost way to learn what else is available. Fidelity Funding's initial review uses a soft credit pull, so exploring does not affect your score.

Whichever route you choose, ask for the total payback in writing, the payment schedule, every fee, and any guarantee or collateral requirement. Walk away from anyone who rushes you or promises outcomes they cannot control.

One more check: ask both types of provider about prepayment. A direct lender and a funding partner may both give you a discount or no discount for paying early, and the answer can change which offer is actually cheapest if you expect to repay ahead of schedule.

key_takeaways: Direct lenders can be cheaper and simpler when you fit their standard profile.
Brokers give reach: one application can reach several funding partners with different appetites.
Broker compensation should be disclosed and can add to cost, so compare total payback.
Applying to many lenders alone can mean multiple inquiries and lost time.
Start with your own bank if your profile is conventional, and use a broker if you need options or speed.

faq.q: Is it cheaper to go directly to a lender?
faq.a: It can be, because there is no broker commission in the price. But a broker may reach funding partners whose terms are better for your profile than the one lender you would have tried. Compare total payback on every offer, whichever route produced it.

faq.q: Can I use both a broker and apply directly?
faq.a: Yes, but coordinate. Applying to the same lender both directly and through a broker can create duplicate submissions and confusion. Tell your specialist about any applications already in progress so they can avoid overlap.

faq.q: Do brokers only offer expensive funding?
faq.a: Not necessarily. The range depends on the funding partners and on your profile. Some products are more expensive because they move faster or accept more risk. A good broker shows the total cost of each offer and explains the trade-off instead of hiding it.

faq.q: Who do I make payments to if I use a broker?
faq.a: Normally the funding partner that issued the funds, not the broker. The agreement you sign names the funding partner and sets out the payment terms. Confirm this in writing before signing.

faq.q: When should I skip a broker?
faq.a: If you have strong credit, plenty of time and a bank that already knows you, a direct application may be simplest and cheapest. Brokers tend to be most useful when your situation is unusual, urgent or you want multiple offers to compare.
